prize_parts.citation: For establishing the concepts, theory and mechanistic framework of proton-coupled electron transfer in chemical and biological energy conversion

statement.case_for: Proton-coupled electron transfer is a physical principle, not a technique: it explains how respiration, photosynthesis and water oxidation move protons and electrons together, and it underlies molecular electrocatalysis for fuels. Mayer's bond-strength thermochemistry and concerted-PCET framework, Hammes-Schiffer's quantum treatment of the proton that made the couplings quantitative, and Nocera's PCET view of water oxidation and artificial photosynthesis form a coherent experiment-plus-theory triad. The concept has been confirmed over decades, is standard in teaching and in enzyme mechanism work, and so recognition would be timely rather than premature. I weigh it as the strongest conceptual chemistry on the list. I declare that it sits near my own field and that I may be overrating its centrality.
statement.case_against: The topic reads as a broad field rather than one discovery, T. J. Meyer's foundational work forces an awkward choice in a three-person cut, and its first-place support is thin: one first place and 8 Borda points, against 47 for B063. Some enzymatic PCET claims remain debated in detail. If the committee wants a single crisp, widely visible achievement with clear credit, the protein-degradation candidate has more support and a more obvious pharmacological payoff.

responses.point: Targeted protein degradation (B063) is conceptually original, reframes undruggable targets, and is the top choice, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as laureates.
responses.response: I agree B063 is original chemistry and it was my own second choice, so I do not see it as weak. I disagree that it is the clearly prior choice. The prize would have to decide between the PROTAC concept (Crews, Deshaies) and the cereblon and molecular-glue mechanism (Handa, Ito), and Ciulli's VHL work is also not marginal, so a three-name cut leaves out people whose contributions are not minor. You call it slightly early, and I would stress that no PROTAC drug is yet approved. I would support it if the committee can define one core achievement, but I would not treat opening first places as scientific merit.

responses.point: Massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis (B031) is chemistry at its core (reversible terminators, surface attachment, single-molecule detection), and Balasubramanian and Klenerman are the decisive pair.
responses.response: The chemistry of reversible terminators is real and I do not dispute the impact. My reservations are attribution and category. Priority among Solexa, 454 (Rothberg) and the Ju and Mayer platforms is commercially entangled, as you note yourself. The result is also read mostly as enabling technology for genomics and medicine, with Sanger's prize in 1980 as precedent. I would put it below a concept-level contribution such as PCET, but I accept that on technology-driven fields we may weigh maturity differently.

responses.point: Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling (B032) is a general, step-economical method in daily industrial use, with Buchwald and Hartwig as clear laureates.
responses.response: I agree the attribution is cleaner than for most candidates, and the impact is not in doubt. My main reservation is that the 2010 cross-coupling prize already honoured the Pd-catalysed bond-forming paradigm, and this would look like an extension of it, even if the C-N variant is a real advance. I would credit Kosugi explicitly if the committee goes this way. For me the question is novelty of principle, and there I put PCET ahead.

responses.point: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B035) turned lipid self-assembly and bilayer phase behaviour into a deliverable medicine platform, an instance of physical chemistry.
responses.response: The physical-chemistry argument is persuasive, and the pKa-tuned design principle is original. Societal impact is enormous. My concern is that credit across Vancouver, the Boston lipidoid line and industry is partly settled by patent disputes, and the 2023 Medicine prize already honoured the mRNA side of the same story. I would keep B035 as a serious contender but not as my first choice.

uncertainties: Whether T. J. Meyer's foundational contribution should displace one of Mayer, Hammes-Schiffer and Nocera.
Whether PCET will be read by colleagues as one coherent discovery or a broad field.
Whether the committee will accept the experiment-theory split among the three PCET laureates.
How the committee weighs the Medicine-adjacent overlap of the biomedical candidates (B063, B035) against more fundamental chemistry.
statement.conflict_note: No institutional conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from the profile; I am Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, who ranked other candidates. My research on proton transfer in respiratory enzymes is scientifically close to B025 (PCET), so I disclose this proximity and ask colleagues to weigh my enthusiasm accordingly, though no recusal seems necessary.
